Episode Title: The Hidden Emotional Labour of School Staff (And Why It’s Breaking You)
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, stress management, communication, education, screen time, identity and belonging
Show Notes:
Teachers and school staff are walking out of buildings every day completely exhausted — not because the day was dramatic, but because it was relentless.

In this episode, Ashley explores the hidden emotional labour happening inside schools — the constant co-regulation, emotional containment, and nervous system management that rarely gets acknowledged but leaves staff mentally and physically depleted.

If you’re a teacher, TA, SENCO, pastoral lead, or school-based professional who goes home emotionally drained, unable to switch off, or snapping at the people you love — this episode explains why.

With honesty, professional insight, and practical guidance, Ashley breaks down what emotional labour really looks like in schools, why the most compassionate staff are at greatest risk of burnout, and how small nervous system shifts can protect your wellbeing without asking you to care less.

In this episode, we cover:

  • What emotional labour in schools really means (and why it’s invisible)
  • Why supporting dysregulated children drains your nervous system
  • The difference between being busy-tired and emotionally exhausted
  • Why compassionate, emotionally attuned staff are most at risk of burnout
  • The difference between empathy and emotional absorbing
  • Why burnout isn’t weakness — it’s sustained emotional output
  • How the education system contributes to staff depletion
  • The identity shift school professionals need to protect themselves

Why school staff feel so drained

Supporting children with behaviour, regulation, trauma, and emotional needs requires constant calm tone, steady presence, and emotional containment. Staff regulate multiple nervous systems before they even reach their own.

Over time, without space to reset, this creates nervous system overload.

This isn’t about resilience.

This isn’t about being “stronger.”

This is sustained emotional output without protection.

Practical takeaways:

  • Separate empathy from absorbing — ask “Is this mine or theirs?”
  • Close emotional loops after difficult moments
  • Use small nervous system resets between interactions
  • Build one low-demand moment into your day
  • Name the emotional load instead of suppressing it
  • Create transition rituals before going home
  • Use predictability to reduce emotional firefighting
  • Remember that presence doesn’t mean perfection

Key reminder:

You are not burning out because you are weak.

You are burning out because you care deeply inside a system that rarely slows down.

The goal is not to care less.

The goal is to protect yourself while you care.

Who This Episode Is For:

  • Teachers and teaching assistants
  • SENCOs and pastoral leads
  • School leaders and SLT
  • School-based therapists and professionals
  • Anyone working with children who feels emotionally depleted

Episode Title: The One Who Advocated
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, school wellbeing, confidence, mental health, education, family relationships
Show Notes:
We often hear the phrase “It takes a village to raise a child.” And while community matters, research consistently shows something powerful: the single greatest protective factor in a child’s life is one stable, supportive adult.

One person who believes in them.
One person who advocates for them.
One person who stays steady when life feels uncertain.

This episode launches a brand-new series on The Resilient Kid Podcast called Only Takes One Person.

Fresh off the stage after winning the Heart of the Community Award, Ashley reflects on the power of advocacy, connection, and the ripple effect one person can have on a life.

In this opening episode, Ashley shares a deeply personal story about her Auntie Vera (Vee) — the woman who stepped in and advocated for her when she was just 21 years old.

After finishing her psychology degree, Ashley had applied for a counselling course, only to be told she was too young to be accepted. While Ashley was travelling in South America, her Auntie Vee received the call from the course professor.

Rather than accepting the decision quietly, Vee stood up for her niece.

She explained the experiences Ashley had already navigated in life — growing up in a multi-generational family, supporting grandparents, and witnessing her father’s mental health struggles — and why those experiences had shaped her desire to help others.

That moment of advocacy changed everything.

Ashley became the youngest person ever accepted onto the course, beginning a journey that has now spanned 30 years of supporting children, families and schools.

But this episode isn’t just about one phone call.

It’s about the profound impact one person can have on a young life.

Whether that person is a parent, teacher, mentor, coach or relative — a single relationship can change a child’s sense of safety, belief, and possibility.

Through The Resilient Kid programme, Ashley and her team hope to be that person for many of the children and families they support.

Because sometimes, the biggest changes begin with the smallest moments of belief.

In this episode, we explore:

  • Why one supportive adult is the strongest protective factor for children
  • A personal story about advocacy and opportunity
  • How belief from others shapes confidence and resilience
  • Why the work of supporting children is often about showing up consistently
  • The ripple effect one person can create across a lifetime

A reflection for listeners

  • Who was the person who believed in you?
  • A parent, teacher, coach, mentor, grandparent or friend who saw something in you before you fully saw it yourself?
  • We would love to hear your story.
  • Because resilience isn’t built in isolation.
    It’s built in connection.
  • And sometimes… it only takes one person.

Episode Title: The Place I Finally Fit
Topics: resilience, friendships, stress management, communication, mental health, education, identity and belonging, personal growth
Show Notes:
"You made this place look like somewhere worth being."

Can I ask you something personal?

When did you first feel like you belonged somewhere?

Not tolerated. Not managed. Not just allowed to be in the room. But actually belonging. Like the space would feel different if you weren't in it. Like you were expected. Wanted. Part of something.

For some of you, that feeling showed up early. A family dinner table, a school team, a childhood bedroom that felt like the whole world.

But for a lot of people — more than we talk about — that feeling took a long time to arrive. And when it did, it didn't come from where they expected.

It came from one person. One adult who decided, without being asked, without it being in their job description, without any guarantee of it working — that this kid was worth showing up for.

Today we're talking about those people. The youth workers. The support workers. The ones who sit in community centres and church halls and temporary offices with bad lighting and somehow — they change everything.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Kezia is thirteen. She has been to four schools in five years. She eats lunch in the library. She draws entire cities in the margins of her notebooks — intricate, detailed, worlds she has been quietly building for two years — and she has never shown anyone.

Then one Thursday afternoon she ends up at a youth centre she doesn't want to be in. And a youth worker called Marcus asks her one question about her drawing that nobody has ever thought to ask.

This is the story of what happened next. And it's the story of why one adult, in an underfunded room with a broken table tennis table, can change the entire direction of a child's life.

This episode is for anyone who has ever felt like they didn't quite fit anywhere. And it's for every youth worker, support worker, and community professional who shows up anyway — week after week — even when no one seems to be watching.

RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Belonging Uncertainty Researcher Gregory Walton at Stanford University found that for young people who have experienced instability or rejection, there is a persistent internal question running like background noise — "Do I belong here? Is this temporary? Will this be taken away?" This belonging uncertainty takes up cognitive and emotional space, making it harder to connect, engage, and learn. Even small moments of genuine human acknowledgement were shown to reduce belonging uncertainty and significantly improve wellbeing and engagement. ?? Gregory Walton — Belonging research, Stanford University

Fitting In Is Not Belonging Dr. Brené Brown's research on vulnerability makes a crucial distinction: fitting in is assessing a situation and becoming who you need to be to be accepted. Belonging is being accepted as you already are. Children who feel they don't belong often exhaust themselves trying to fit in — which actually moves them further from the genuine connection they're craving. ?? Brown, B. — The Gifts of Imperfection (Hazelden Publishing)

The Power of One Stable Adult Research by Save the Children UK and the Centre for Research on Families and Relationships found that for children experiencing family instability — frequent moves, parental stress, inconsistent caregiving — the single most protective factor against long-term mental health difficulties was the presence of at least one stable, consistent, non-family adult relationship. Not therapy. Not programmes. One person. Showing up. ?? Save the Children UK / Centre for Research on Families and Relationships

The Youth Work Funding Crisis The National Youth Agency estimates that local authority spending on youth services in England fell by over 70% between 2010 and 2020. Thousands of centres closed. Hundreds of thousands of young people lost access to youth workers. And yet research by Catch22 found that for every pound invested in youth work, there is an estimated return of over four pounds in reduced costs to public services — mental health support, criminal justice, welfare. ?? National Youth Agency — NYA Home - National Youth Agency ?? Catch22 — Home | Catch22

FIVE WAYS TO CREATE BELONGING FOR A CHILD WHO HAS LEARNED TO DISAPPEAR

  • Enter through their interest, not their story — Don't lead with what you know about their background. Ask about what they care about. Their interests are the door. Trust comes later.

  • Don't reward disclosure — reward presence — When a withdrawn child shows up, that is brave. You don't need them to open up straight away. Let presence be enough at first. Say "good to see you" and mean it.

  • Be boringly consistent — Same hello, every week. Remember the small things they mentioned last time. For a child whose life has been unpredictable, your consistency is a gift. Predictability is safety. Safety is belonging.

  • Let them contribute — Belonging isn't just about being received, it's about having something to give. Find ways for the child to contribute. The moment they feel "this place needs something from me" is the moment they start to feel part of it.

  • Name the belonging out loud — Don't assume they feel it. Say it explicitly. "This group is better when you're here." Children who have learned to disappear often need the belonging spelled out. Give them the words.

Episode Title: Someone Finally Stayed
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, school wellbeing, confidence, communication, mental health, education
Show Notes:
"No one's ever actually said that to me before."

In all the years I've been doing this work — sitting with young people and their families, walking into schools, being in the rooms where the real conversations happen — there is one thing that comes up more than any technique, any model, any framework.

People heal when they feel safe enough to be honest. And they feel safe enough to be honest when someone has shown them — consistently, over time — that they are not going anywhere.

At The Resilient Kid, everything we do comes back to two things. We meet young people where they are. Not where we need them to be, not where the curriculum says they should be — where they actually are, right now, in this moment. And we wrap around them 360 degrees. Because a young person doesn't exist in isolation. They exist in a family, in a school, in a community. And real change happens when everyone around that young person is working together.

Today I want to tell you what that looks like in practice. This is Ryan's story.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Ryan was fourteen when he came to us. He didn't come willingly. Hood up, arms folded, absolutely certain this wasn't going to work. His dad had left when he was seven — not with a dramatic moment, just a slow fade — and for seven years Ryan had been quietly carrying a question he had never said out loud to anyone: what did I do wrong?

His mum was loving and exhausted and stuck in a cycle she hadn't chosen. His school described him as fine. And fine, in our experience, is one of the most worrying words there is.

This episode is about what happened when we met Ryan where he was, wrapped around his whole world — therapy room, family home, school corridor — and stayed. It's about the moment he started to believe, not in the process, but in himself.

And it's about why healing never happens in isolation. It happens in relationship. Every time.

RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

The Therapeutic Relationship Is the Intervention A landmark meta-analysis by John Norcross — one of the world's leading researchers in psychotherapy outcomes — found that the therapeutic alliance accounts for as much as 30% of the variance in therapy outcomes. More than the model used. More than any specific technique. The relationship itself is the mechanism of change. For young people, especially, this is amplified — adolescence is developmentally defined by the question: can I trust you? ?? Norcross, J.C. — Psychotherapy Relationships That Work (APA, 2011)

Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory Professor Urie Bronfenbrenner's theory tells us that a child's development is shaped by the interaction between all the systems around them — family, school, community, culture. A child who is struggling is not struggling in a vacuum. Intervening in only one system is like mopping the floor without turning off the tap. This is the clinical foundation of the 360 wrap — working across every system, with every key adult, at the same time. ?? Bronfenbrenner, U. — The Ecology of Human Development (Harvard University Press, 1979)

Resilience and the Adult Network Research by Professor Michael Rutter on childhood resilience found that the most resilient young people — those who navigated serious adversity and came through it — almost universally had one thing in common: a network of consistent, communicating adults who held them together. Not one hero. A network. A wrap. ?? Rutter, M. — Resilience research, Institute of Psychiatry, London

See. Safe. Connect. Heal. Dan Siegel, clinical professor of psychiatry at UCLA, describes the sequence that makes healing possible: you have to be seen to feel safe, you have to feel safe to connect, and you have to connect to heal. You cannot skip a step. This sequence sits at the heart of everything we do at The Resilient Kid — and it's why we work across the therapy room, the family, and the school at the same time. ?? Siegel, D. — The Developing Mind (Guilford Press)

Youth Mental Health in the UK One in six children aged five to sixteen in the UK now meets the criteria for a mental health condition. In many areas, CAMHS referral waiting times exceed a year. In the gap between crisis and support, young people are sitting in classrooms and at dinner tables carrying things that are too heavy for one person to carry alone. This is the gap The Resilient Kid works in — every single day.

?? NHS Digital — Mental Health of Children and Young People in England (2022) ?? YoungMinds — YoungMinds | Mental Health Charity For Children And Young People

THE 360 WRAP IN PRACTICE — FIVE PRINCIPLES

  • Meet them where they are, not where you need them to be — Before any session or conversation, ask: where is this young person right now, today? Not on paper. Not last week. Right now. Start there. Always.

  • Curiosity before conclusion — When behaviour is challenging, get curious before you get corrective. What is this communicating? What is the need underneath it? Behaviour is always a message. Our job is to learn the language.

  • Make the invisible visible — gently — Many young people have never had words for what they feel. Part of the work is slowly giving them a vocabulary. Not labelling. Not diagnosing in front of them. Naming things alongside them, so they begin to understand their own internal world.

  • Get the adults talking to each other — With appropriate consent, therapists should talk to schools and families. Share the language. Create consistency across every system around the young person. When the adults in a child's life are connected and communicating, the child feels held — even when they don't know that's what's happening.

  • Repair is part of the relationship, not a sign it's broken — There will be hard sessions. Weeks when a young person pushes you away. Stay. Repair. Come back. For young people whose attachment history has taught them that relationships end when things get hard, your willingness to stay through the difficult moments is itself the intervention.

Episode Title: The Science of Small Things
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, school wellbeing, stress management, communication, mental health
Show Notes:
"The small things are not the consolation prize when the big things aren't available. The small things are the thing."

It's Mental Health Week. And this episode is not going to tell you to do more.

It's not going to give you a seventeen step programme or add to the already very long list of things you feel like you should be doing and aren't quite managing. Because the science — and we are going to get into the science properly today — doesn't point to more as the answer.

It points to the breakfast table. The school gate hello. The named feeling. The repair after the hard moment. The predictable ritual before bed.

The things that most of you — parents, teachers, the people who love children and show up for them every single day — are already doing without realising it counts.

Nobody told you it counted. This episode does.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

One in six children in England aged five to sixteen meets the criteria for a probable mental health condition. CAMHS waiting lists in many areas stretch beyond a year. And in response we keep searching for bigger solutions — more programmes, more training, more resources for already stretched professionals and exhausted parents.

All of which have value. But in the search for the big solution we have consistently overlooked something the research has been quietly pointing to for decades. The most powerful protective factors for children's mental health are not clinical. They are not expensive. They do not require a referral or a waiting list or a specialist.

They are the small, repeated, ordinary interactions between a child and a trusted adult. And they are doing something extraordinary inside a child's brain and body — whether we realise it or not.

This Mental Health Week special brings together the science, the stories, and the practical tools to show parents and teachers alike that what they are already doing matters more than they know. Because the most important message we can send this Mental Health Week is not do more. It is this: you are already doing more than you know.

02:00 — Why we've been looking in the wrong direction 06:00 — The science: What small things actually do in a child's brain

?? RESEARCH AND CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Serve and Return — Harvard Center on the Developing Child Every time a child sends out a signal — a look, a sound, a gesture, a behaviour — and a responsive adult returns it with warmth and acknowledgement, a neural pathway is strengthened. These tiny back and forth interactions, repeated thousands of times across a childhood, build the neurological foundations of emotional regulation, communication, and resilience. It is not a programme. It is a conversation. It is already happening — and it is already working.
?? Center on the Developing Child at Harvard University

The Stress Buffering Adult — Dr. Charles Nelson, Harvard Medical School When a child experiences stress in the presence of a supportive, responsive adult, the stress response is physiologically buffered. The cortisol spike is blunted. The nervous system returns to baseline more quickly. Over time, the child's own stress regulation system becomes stronger and more resilient. The adult doesn't have to do anything dramatic. They just have to be present, regulated, and noticing.

The ACE Study — Adverse Childhood Experiences One of the largest investigations of childhood trauma ever conducted found that adversity in childhood has real, measurable long-term effects on health and wellbeing. What gets talked about far less is the equally robust finding on the other side: a trusted, consistent adult in a child's life significantly buffers against those effects — even in the presence of serious adversity. The buffering agent is not a specialist intervention. It is a person. Showing up. In small and ordinary ways.
?? Felitti, V.J. et al. (1998) — American Journal of Preventive Medicine

Dr. Nadine Burke Harris — The Deepest Well The dose of adversity matters. And so does the dose of protection. Warm, predictable, consistent relationships are the most powerful protective factor we have for children facing difficulty — more powerful, and more accessible, than any clinical intervention.
?? Burke Harris, N. — The Deepest Well (Bluebird, 2018)

Emotional Coaching — Dr. John Gottman Children whose parents acknowledged and named their emotions — rather than dismissing or minimising them — showed significantly better outcomes across every measure of wellbeing, including emotional regulation, social skills, academic achievement, and physical health. The intervention was not complex. When your child feels something, name it alongside them. One sentence. Repeated across a childhood. That is emotional intelligence being built in real time.
?? Gottman, J. — Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child (Simon & Schuster, 1997)

Rupture and Repair — Ed Tronick Tronick's still-face paradigm research shows that it is not the absence of rupture that builds secure attachment — it is the presence of repair. Children do not need perfect adults. They need adults who, when they get it wrong, come back. Say sorry. Try again. The repair is the message: this relationship is stronger than the hard moment. You are safe here even when things go wrong.

Polyvagal Theory — Stephen Porges Nervous systems are contagious. A regulated adult in the room regulates the room. When you are calm, present, and grounded the children around you feel it in their bodies before a word is said. Your state is the most powerful tool you have — in the therapy room, the classroom, and the kitchen.
?? Porges, S. — The Pocket Guide to the Polyvagal Theory (W.W. Norton, 2017)

Virginia Satir — Human Connection and Touch Satir's research on human connection highlighted the profound role of physical warmth in signalling safety and belonging. A hug, a hand on the shoulder, a moment of physical warmth releases oxytocin in both giver and receiver — literally telling the nervous system: you are safe here.
?? Satir, V. — The New Peoplemaking (Science and Behaviour Books, 1988)

THE FIVE SMALL THINGS — WHAT THEY ARE AND WHAT THEY DO

  • The Twenty Second Hug: Physical warmth releases oxytocin in both giver and receiver, signalling safety to the nervous system. Twenty seconds is long enough to feel it. You have twenty seconds, even on the hardest Wednesday morning.

  • The Transition Check-In: The school run, the school gate, the moment a child comes home — these are neurologically significant moments of state change. A warm, present acknowledgement lands deepest here. Not "how was your day" but something smaller and realer. "I missed you today." Eye contact. Thirty seconds.

  • The Named Feeling: When a child is upset or overwhelmed, name what you see before you fix or correct anything. "You seem really overwhelmed right now." One sentence. It tells the child: your inner world is real, it is visible, and it is not too much for me. That experience, repeated across time, is the foundation of emotional regulation.

  • The Predictable Ritual: Bedtime. Breakfast. The same song in the car. The joke only your family knows. Rituals are neurologically soothing because they are predictable — and predictability is safety. For a child whose nervous system is always asking what comes next, a ritual answers before the question is asked.

  • The Repair: When you get it wrong — and you will, because you are human — come back. Say sorry. Try again. Children do not need perfect adults. They need adults who return. The repair is not the failure. The repair is the lesson: you are safe here, even when things go wrong.

FOR THE TEACHERS — YOUR FOUR SMALL THINGS

Use their name warmly. Not as a correction or a warning — just warmly, in passing. Being called by name activates a sense of being known and belonging that is neurologically significant.

Notice the quiet ones. The children who present no trouble and take up no space are not fine by definition. They may be managing. A quiet check-in takes ten seconds and can be the only moment in a child's day where an adult chose to see them.

Regulate yourself first. Nervous systems are contagious. A calm, grounded adult regulates the room before a word is spoken. Your state is your most powerful classroom tool.

Acknowledge without fixing. When a child comes in carrying something heavy, you don't have to solve it. "Looks like today's a tough one. I've got you." That is enough. Sometimes that is everything.

Episode Title: The Moment They Let Me In
Topics: resilience, parenting, school wellbeing, boundaries, mental health, education, personal growth, relationships
Show Notes:
"Trust is not given. It is earned. Slowly, quietly, in the accumulation of ordinary moments."

In all the years I've been doing this work — sitting with young people and their families, walking into schools, being in the rooms where the real conversations happen — there is one thing that comes up more than any technique, any model, any framework.

People heal when they feel safe enough to be honest. And they feel safe enough to be honest when someone has shown them — consistently, over time — that they are not going anywhere.

At The Resilient Kid we meet young people where they are. Not where we need them to be. Not where the curriculum says they should be. Where they actually are, right now, in this moment. And we wrap around them 360 degrees — therapy room, family home, school corridor — because real change happens when everyone around that young person is working together.

But before any of that can work, something else has to come first.

Trust.

This episode is about what it actually takes to build it with a young person who has every reason not to give it. And about the moment — on a grey Tuesday afternoon, walking side by side with a hot chocolate going cold in a paper cup — when Mia finally let us in.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Mia was fifteen when she came to us. By that point she had been seen by four different services in three years. A school counsellor who left. A CAMHS referral that led to a waiting list and then a discharge. A voluntary sector worker who lost her funding. A social worker who changed three times in eighteen months.

Four services. Three years. Not one consistent face.

What that does to a young person is not just leave them without support. It teaches them something. It teaches them that adults come and go. That the moment you start to trust someone — the moment you let them see a little of what is actually going on — they leave. And so Mia had learned, not consciously but in her bones, to give just enough to keep things moving. Never enough to risk anything real.

This episode is about what happened when we stopped trying to break through the wall and started sitting alongside it instead. It is about Brené Brown's BRAVING framework and what it tells us about why trust is so hard to rebuild once it has been broken. It is about the neuroscience of why a walk and a hot chocolate can do what a therapy room sometimes cannot. And it is about the moment Mia asked the most vulnerable question she knew how to ask — and what we said back.

This one is for every professional who has ever sat with a young person who wouldn't let them in. And for every young person who has learned, through painful experience, that letting people in is not safe.

It doesn't have to stay that way.

TIMESTAMPS

02:00 — Mia's Story, Part One — four services, three years, not one consistent face
07:00 — The Research: Polyvagal Theory, walk and talk therapy, and Brené Brown's BRAVING inventory
14:00 — Top Tips: Building trust with a young person who has every reason not to

RESEARCH AND CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Polyvagal Theory — Stephen Porges Our nervous system is constantly reading cues of safety and danger in our environment, and the physiological state we are in determines what we are capable of emotionally. For a young person like Mia, a therapy room had become a cue for guardedness — triggering a low-level threat response that kept part of her brain scanning for danger rather than available for honest, reflective conversation. You cannot think your way into feeling safe. Safety has to be felt in the body first.
?? Porges, S. — The Pocket Guide to the Polyvagal Theory (W.W. Norton, 2017)

Walk and Talk Therapy — Nature, Movement and the Therapeutic Relationship When we walk alongside someone rather than sitting across from them, the face-to-face dynamic — which for a guarded young person can feel like being watched and assessed — is removed. Side by side is the position of accompaniment, not examination. Movement also activates bilateral stimulation of the body which reduces emotional arousal and increases access to reflective thinking. And being outside disrupts the learned cue of the therapy room, creating a gap in which something real can slip through. ?? Jordan, M. and Hinds, J. — Ecotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice (Palgrave Macmillan, 2016)
?? van der Kolk, B. — The Body Keeps the Score (Penguin, 2014)

Brené Brown — The BRAVING Inventory Brown's research found that trust is not built in grand gestures or single defining moments. It is built in the smallest of moments. Quietly. Over time. Her BRAVING inventory breaks trust down into seven specific elements — and when mapped onto the experience of a young person who has been passed from service to service, it shows exactly what has been broken and exactly what needs to be rebuilt.

B — Boundaries. Do you respect my boundaries and honour yours?
R — Reliability. Do you do what you say you will do, consistently, over time?
A — Accountability. When you make a mistake, do you own it and make it right?
V — Vault. Do you keep what I share with you confidential? Is my story safe with you?
I — Integrity. Do you choose courage over comfort? Do you practise your values?
N — Non-judgement. Can I tell you how I feel without being judged for it?
G — Generosity. Do you extend the most generous interpretation to my intentions?

For Mia, every single one of these elements had been undermined — not by bad people, but by a broken system. And this is what the therapeutic relationship at The Resilient Kid was quietly, consistently rebuilding. One element at a time. Starting with reliability.
?? Brown, B. — Daring Greatly (Penguin, 2012)
?? Brown, B. — The Gifts of Imperfection (Hazelden Publishing, 2010)

Attachment Theory — Mary Ainsworth Secure attachment — the experience of having a safe base — is built through repeated experiences of a caregiver being present, responsive, and consistent. For young people like Mia whose experience of adults has been anything but consistent, the therapeutic relationship has to do reparative attachment work. It has to become, over time, the safe base that was never reliably there. Safe bases are not built in sixty-minute weekly sessions alone. They are built in the accumulation of small moments.
?? Ainsworth, M. — Patterns of Attachment (Lawrence Erlbaum, 1978)

Breaks in Provision — Children's Commissioner for England Research by the Children's Commissioner has found that a significant proportion of young people referred to mental health services experience at least one break in provision before reaching stable support. Each break is not just an inconvenience. Each break is a lesson. And the lesson is: don't bother trusting.
?? Homepage | Children's Commissioner for England

CAMHS Waiting Times In many areas of England CAMHS waiting lists currently stretch to eighteen months. Voluntary sector services — often the most relational and flexible, and most able to reach young people like Mia — are chronically underfunded and first to face cuts when budgets tighten.
?? YoungMinds — YoungMinds | Mental Health Charity For Children And Young People ?? NHS Digital — Mental Health of Children and Young People in England (2022)

FIVE WAYS TO BUILD TRUST WITH A YOUNG PERSON WHO HAS EVERY REASON NOT TO

  • Don't take the wall personally The wall was built before you arrived, by experiences that had nothing to do with you. Your job is not to demolish it. Your job is to be so consistently, boringly safe that the young person eventually decides — on their own terms, in their own time — that they don't need it quite so high around you.

  • Match your energy to theirs, not your agenda If they come in flat, sit in the flat with them. If they're closed, don't push for open. Meet them exactly where they are and let them feel that wherever they are is acceptable. There is no wrong way to show up here.

  • Do things side by side, not face to face Walk. Make something. Look at something together. Side by side says: I am not watching you. I am with you. For a young person who is used to being assessed, that is a completely different experience.

  • Name the pattern without blame When the time is right, name what has happened to them. "I know you've been here before. With other people. And I know they didn't stay. I want you to know that I know that — and I'm not going anywhere." Then prove it. Week after week. By still being there.

  • Let the small moments be enough Not every session will feel significant. Some will feel like nothing happened. Trust the accumulation. Trust that showing up, being consistent, and remembering the small things is doing something — even when it doesn't look like it. The walk with the hot chocolate looked like nothing. It was everything.

Episode Title: Building Wellbeing Communities for Kids & Families
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, friendships, confidence, mindfulness, stress management, mental health
Show Notes:
Ashley is joined by Neil Lewis (The Empathy Coach) and Becky Percival (Rebecca Percival Coaching), the co-founders of the Warrington Wellbeing Festival, for a warm, inspiring conversation about why community wellbeing matters, what it means to future-proof our children, and why they’ve built something truly special in the heart of Warrington.

Episode Title: The Anxiety I Didn't Know I Was Giving You
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, school wellbeing, bullying, stress management, communication
Show Notes:
"I think this is me. I think I gave this to them."

I want to ask you something that takes a bit of courage to answer honestly.

When your child is anxious — when the stomachaches appear on Monday mornings, when the worries multiply overnight, when the school gate becomes a battleground — where do you look for the reason?

Most of us look outward. School. Friends. Screens. The state of the world.

But sometimes — and I say this with every ounce of compassion I have — sometimes the thing that is making a child anxious is closer to home than that. Sometimes it is in the air of the house itself. In the quality of a Sunday evening silence. In the tightness of a parent's shoulders at breakfast.

Anxiety is one of the most contagious things there is. It moves through families like weather. And most of the time the parent passing it on has absolutely no idea it is happening.

This episode is for every parent who has ever sat across from me and said — with tears in their eyes and shock in their voice — I think this is me. I think I gave this to them.

It happens more than you know. And it is never too late to do something about it.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Claire came to us because her daughter Ellie — nine years old, bright, imaginative, funny — had started refusing to go to school. Stomachaches on Monday mornings. Tears at the school gate. A growing list of worries that seemed to multiply overnight.

Claire had done everything right. She had listened, validated, spoken to the teacher, tried the breathing exercises. She loved Ellie with everything she had and she was exhausted and frightened and utterly at a loss.

When I asked her how she felt on Monday mornings, she laughed — a short, surprised laugh. Awful, she said. She had hated Mondays her whole life. And when Ellie came down for breakfast, she found her mum already tense, already quiet, already in her head.

That oh moment — the sound of something clicking into place — is where this episode begins.

This is not an episode about blame. It is an episode about what the science tells us about how anxiety travels through families without a word being spoken, why a parent's unexamined anxiety is one of the strongest predictors of childhood anxiety there is, and — most importantly — what happens when a parent decides to do something about it. Not just for themselves. For the child they love.

?? RESEARCH AND CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Right Brain to Right Brain Communication — Allan Schore Research by neurobiologist Allan Schore shows that in the early years of life a child's nervous system literally co-regulates with their parent's. The parent's calm is the child's calm. The parent's anxiety is the child's anxiety. This attunement is so finely calibrated that a child can detect a shift in their parent's emotional state before that parent has said a single word or changed a single behaviour. And it does not stop at babyhood. It continues throughout childhood and adolescence. It is always happening. ?? Schore, A. — The Science of the Art of Psychotherapy (W.W. Norton, 2012)

Polyvagal Theory — Stephen Porges Our nervous systems are constantly reading cues of safety and danger in the environment. For young children, the most powerful cue in the environment is not a sound or a situation — it is the nervous system of their primary caregiver. A regulated parent regulates the room. An anxious parent activates it. ?? Porges, S. — The Pocket Guide to the Polyvagal Theory (W.W. Norton, 2017)

Parental Anxiety and Childhood Anxiety — Professor Lynne Murray Research by Professor Lynne Murray at the University of Reading shows that parental anxiety is one of the strongest predictors of childhood anxiety. Not because anxious parents are bad parents — they are often extraordinarily attentive and loving. But anxiety changes behaviour in ways that can unintentionally communicate danger to a child. Over-reassurance signals the worry was real. Over-protection deprives a child of the experience of coping. Modelled avoidance teaches avoidance. None of it is conscious. All of it can be changed. ?? Murray, L. — The Psychology of Babies (Robinson, 2014)

Intergenerational Transmission — Daniel Siegel and Mary Hartzell Siegel and Hartzell's landmark research found that it is not what happened to us in our childhoods that determines how we parent. It is whether we have made sense of what happened to us. Parents who had difficult childhoods but had processed those experiences — who had developed what Siegel calls a coherent narrative about their own lives — parented just as securely as parents who had easy childhoods. Doing your own work is not just good for you. It is one of the most powerful things you can do for your child. ?? Siegel, D. and Hartzell, M. — Parenting from the Inside Out (Scribe, 2004)

Intergenerational Trauma — Mark Wolynn Wolynn's work on intergenerational trauma shows how unprocessed experiences are passed down through families — not through DNA alone but through behaviour, atmosphere, and the emotional language of the home. His central message: the greatest gift you can give your child is to heal yourself. ?? Wolynn, M. — It Didn't Start With You (Penguin, 2016)

?? FIVE THINGS TO DO WHEN YOU RECOGNISE YOURSELF IN YOUR CHILD'S STRUGGLE

  • Get curious, not guilty Guilt is a closed door. Curiosity is an open one. If you recognise that your own anxiety is showing up in your child, the question is not what is wrong with me — it is what happened to me, and how has it shaped the way I move through the world? That question is worth sitting with. And ideally worth exploring with support.

  • Regulate yourself first — always You cannot co-regulate a child from a dysregulated state. Before you try to calm your child, attend to yourself. Breathe. Ground. Notice your own body. This is not selfish. It is the most effective thing you can do. You cannot pour from an empty cup and you cannot offer a nervous system that you haven't first settled yourself.

  • Watch your reassurance Research consistently shows that excessive reassurance actually increases anxiety over time. It tells the child's nervous system that the threat was real enough to need that much reassurance. Instead of reassuring, try validating and then gently encouraging. "I can see you're worried. Worry is really uncomfortable. And I believe you can handle this."

  • Do your own work Not because you are broken. Because you are human. And humans carry things. Getting support — whether that is therapy, coaching, or simply a space to explore your own story — is not a luxury. For a parent whose own wounds are showing up in their child, it is part of the treatment.

  • Tell your child you are working on it too Age appropriately, be honest. "I know I get anxious sometimes and I'm getting some help with that." This normalises help-seeking, reduces the child's sense that they are the problem, and shows them that adults can be self-aware and choose to do something about their struggles. That is one of the greatest gifts you can give.

Episode Title: The Words I Never Had
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, school wellbeing, mental health, education, careers
Show Notes:
"I don't even know what I'm feeling half the time. How am I supposed to help him know what he's feeling?"

OPENING

I want to ask you something.

When you were a child — when you were scared, or sad, or overwhelmed, or angry — what happened?

Not what should have happened. What actually happened.

For some of you, someone came. Someone sat with you and named what you were feeling and made it smaller by being present with it. But for a lot of people — more than we talk about — nobody came. Or somebody came but they fixed and redirected and told you to cheer up or calm down or stop being so sensitive. Or the feeling was met with discomfort, or impatience, or silence. Not because nobody loved you. But because the adults around you hadn't been given the words either.

And so you grew up. And you became a parent. And you looked at this child in front of you — scared or sad or overwhelmed or angry — and you wanted, more than anything, to do it differently. To give them what you didn't have.

And sometimes you didn't know how. Because you had never been shown.

Today's episode is for you.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

David came to us because his son Marcus — twelve years old, football-mad, usually the loudest person in any room — had gone quiet. Withdrawn. Flat. Spending hours in his room. Saying, when asked what was wrong: nothing. I'm fine.

David was a man who loved his son deeply and had absolutely no idea what to do. He sat across from me and said: I'm not really good at this sort of thing. Talking about feelings and that.

When I asked him what he did with difficult feelings as a twelve year old, he didn't hesitate. Kicked a ball. Went to his room. Got on with it.

And then he said something I have never forgotten: I don't even know what I'm feeling half the time. How am I supposed to help him know what he's feeling?

This episode is about that question. About what the science tells us happens when children grow up in homes where emotional language simply isn't spoken. About alexithymia — no words for feelings — and how it travels through generations. And about the remarkable research that shows emotional literacy can be learned at any age. That the brain does not stop being able to form new pathways. That it is never too late to find the words.

This one is for every parent who grew up in a get-on-with-it home and is trying, imperfectly and humanly, to do something different.

TIMESTAMPS

00:00 — Intro: The words we were never given

02:00 — David and Marcus's Story, Part One — I don't know what I'm feeling

07:00 — The Research: Alexithymia, emotional socialisation, and the neuroscience of change

13:00 — Top Tips: Learning the emotional language you were never taught

16:00 — David and Marcus's Story, Part Two — gutting 20:00 — The Bigger Picture: Breaking the chain, one named feeling at a time

22:00 — The Close: Beginnings are everything

24:00 — Outro and resources

?? RESEARCH AND CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Alexithymia — No Words For Feelings Alexithymia — from the Greek, meaning no words for feelings — describes the experience of knowing something feels bad but being unable to identify what the feeling is. Of having an emotion in the body without being able to label it, locate it, or talk about it. Research consistently shows that children who grow up in low emotional expressivity households — where feelings are not named, discussed, or validated — are significantly more likely to develop alexithymic tendencies. It is not a diagnosis. It is a spectrum. And many of us sit somewhere on it without knowing.

?? Professor Mark Taylor — Alexithymia research | University of Toronto

Emotional Socialisation Research by Joseph Ciarrochi and colleagues shows that children learn how to relate to their emotions primarily from watching the adults around them. When a parent dismisses their own emotions — pushing through, getting on with it, not naming what is happening internally — children learn that emotions are things to be managed and suppressed, not felt and expressed. You cannot teach what you were never given. But you can learn it. At any age.

?? Ciarrochi, J. — research on emotional socialisation and childhood wellbeing

Neuroplasticity and Emotional Literacy Daniel Siegel's work on mindsight — the ability to observe and understand your own mental processes — shows that emotional literacy is a skill that can be learned at any age. The brain does not stop being able to form new pathways. A parent who has spent their whole life getting on with it can learn, with the right support, to identify, name, and work with their emotions. And when a parent learns emotional literacy alongside their child, the relational impact is profound. The child sees that it is possible to learn. They see that asking for help is what adults do when they don't know something. They feel less alone.

?? Siegel, D. — Mindsight: The New Science of Personal Transformation (Bantam Books, 2010)

Earned Security — Daniel Siegel and Mary Hartzell Siegel and Hartzell's research introduced the concept of earned security — the process by which adults who did not experience secure attachment in childhood can develop the internal resources of securely attached people through reflective work. You do not have to have had the words to give your child the words. You just have to be willing to find them. Together.

?? Siegel, D. and Hartzell, M. — Parenting from the Inside Out (Scribe, 2004)

Emotion Coaching vs Emotion Dismissing — John Gottman Gottman identified five types of parenting responses to children's emotions. At one end the emotion-dismissing parent — not out of cruelty but because that is all they were ever shown. At the other the emotion-coaching parent — the one who stops, names, validates, and helps the child problem-solve from a place of feeling understood. The distance between those two is not talent or personality. It is awareness and practice. Which means it is available to everyone.

?? Gottman, J. — Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child (Simon & Schuster, 1997)

Intergenerational Transmission — Mark Wolynn Wolynn's research on how unprocessed experiences travel through families shows that the patterns we carry are rarely just ours. They have roots. And when we get curious about those roots — when we make sense of our own story — we break a chain that may have been running for generations.

?? Wolynn, M. — It Didn't Start With You (Penguin, 2016)

Co-Regulation — Allan Schore A child's nervous system co-regulates with their parent's throughout childhood and adolescence. When a parent learns to identify and regulate their own emotions, that regulation becomes available to the child — not just through conversation, but through the quality of presence, atmosphere, and attunement in the home.

?? Schore, A. — The Science of the Art of Psychotherapy (W.W. Norton, 2012)

?? FIVE WAYS TO LEARN THE EMOTIONAL LANGUAGE YOU WERE NEVER TAUGHT

  • Start with yourself, not your child Before you can help your child name their feelings, begin noticing your own. At the end of each day ask yourself three questions: what did I feel today? Where did I feel it in my body? What was happening when I felt it? This is not therapy — it is practice. It builds the muscle.

  • Use a feelings vocabulary — literally There are feelings wheels and feelings charts designed for children that are just as useful for adults who didn't get this early. Print one out. Put it on the fridge. Use it yourself. I think I'm feeling frustrated is a complete sentence. It doesn't have to be profound. It just has to be honest.

  • Name your own feelings out loud in front of your child Not to burden them. Not to overshare. But to model. I'm feeling a bit anxious about that meeting today. I noticed I was irritable this morning and I think I was tired. When a child hears a parent name their own feeling — calmly, simply, without drama — they learn that feelings are normal, nameable things. That is a profound lesson.

  • Repair the dismissals You will get it wrong. You will say calm down or you'll be fine when what was needed was something else. When you notice — even hours later — go back. I said calm down earlier and I don't think that helped. What were you actually feeling? That repair is worth more than getting it right the first time.

  • Do it together Be honest with your child — age appropriately — that you are learning this too. I didn't really grow up talking about feelings but I want us to get better at it together. That honesty changes everything. You are no longer the expert dispensing wisdom from above. You are two people figuring something out side by side. And that is the most powerful position there is.

"The silence is never neutral. It always teaches something. The question is only what."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Welcome to Season 11 of The Resilient Kid — The Talk.

This is our most important season yet. We are spending all ten episodes on the conversations most parents dread and most children desperately need: puberty, periods, consent, and sex.

Why now? Because at The Resilient People — the organisation behind The Resilient Kid and The Resilient Teen — we see the gap every single week. The gap between what young people need to know and what they are actually being told. And in that gap, young people are filling in the blanks themselves — from the internet, from peers, from pornography.

The research is unambiguous. Young people who have ongoing, honest, age-appropriate conversations with trusted adults navigate adolescence with more confidence, more safety, and significantly fewer harms. The conversation is the protection.

So that is what this season is. For parents first — and then, in the second half of the season, directly for young people themselves.

This first episode asks the question underneath all of it: why do we avoid these conversations, what does the silence actually cost our children, and how do we start — even when we don't know how?

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? Where Young People Get Their Information

Research by Brook consistently shows that a significant proportion of young people in the UK identify the internet as their primary source of information about sex and relationships — ahead of parents and schools. In many cases this means exposure to pornography before any educational context has been provided.

?? Brook — Sexual Health & Wellbeing - Brook

?? What Young People Say They Need

The Sex Education Forum's Young People's RSE Poll found that many young people feel their relationships and sex education — both at school and at home — leaves them underprepared. They consistently report wanting more honesty, more real-world relevance, and someone who will talk to them like a real person.

?? Sex Education Forum — sexeducationforum.org.uk

?? The Ofsted Review of Sexual Abuse in Schools (2021)

Ofsted's landmark review found that sexual harassment and abuse among young people — including online — had become normalised in many school environments. Young people reported incidents were so common they had stopped reporting them. The review highlighted the urgent need for high-quality, honest RSE from an early age.

?? Ofsted Review of Sexual Abuse in Schools and Colleges (2021) — Ofsted

?? Shame Is Transmitted, Not Innate

Dr. John Bancroft's research on human sexuality argues that shame around the body and sexuality is not something children are born with. It is learned — transmitted through the discomfort, silence, and subject-changing of the adults around them. Children follow our emotional lead. Our awkwardness teaches them that their bodies and their questions are something to be ashamed of.

?? Bancroft, J. — Human Sexuality and Its Problems (Elsevier, 2008)

?? Language Is Protection — The NSPCC and Talk PANTS

The NSPCC's research underpinning the Talk PANTS campaign demonstrates clearly that children who know the correct anatomical names for their body parts, and who have been given permission to speak about their bodies, are significantly better equipped to recognise and report abuse. Correct language is a safeguarding tool.

?? NSPCC — Healthy relationships | NSPCC
?? Talk PANTS — Talk PANTS: Conversation to help keep children safe | NSPCC

?? The Internet Watch Foundation

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) works to remove child sexual abuse material from the internet and provides guidance to parents on online safety. Their research and parent guidance is clear: open conversation — not restriction alone — is the most effective protection.

?? Internet Watch Foundation — Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation IWF

?? The PSHE Association

The PSHE Association supports schools in delivering high-quality personal, social and health education, including RSE. Their guidance emphasises ongoing, age-appropriate conversation with trusted adults as the strongest protective factor for young people navigating puberty and relationships.

?? PSHE Association — PSHE Association | Charity and membership body for PSHE education

?? FIVE WAYS TO START — QUICK RECAP

  • Start before you're ready

  • — there is no perfect moment. Imperfect and started is better than perfect and never.

  • Use the correct words — penis, vulva, vagina, testicles. Correct anatomical language from the beginning reduces shame and increases safety.

  • Make it ongoing and light — the best conversations happen in car journeys and at breakfast tables. Small and frequent beats big and terrifying.

  • Tell them what you didn't get — honesty about your own experience builds trust and models the courage to try.

Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, friendships, confidence, communication, education
Show Notes:
"He is going to remember that you showed up."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This episode is the practical guide parents have been waiting for — and perhaps dreading.

We follow two families: Marcus, a dad who got through his own puberty in silence and is determined to do it differently for his son Theo; and Priya, a single mum raising her son Jude alone, wondering whether she is the right person to have this conversation at all.

Spoiler: she is. And so are you.

Along the way we cover everything a parent needs to know about male puberty — the timeline, the physical changes, erections, wet dreams, masturbation, and the emotional turbulence that comes with all of it — grounded in research, delivered without shame, with five practical tips for actually making the conversation happen.

?? EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

00:00 Introduction — the question I'm asked more than almost any other
02:00 Marcus and Priya — Part One

?? PUBERTY IN BOYS — WHAT TO EXPECT AND WHEN

Share this section with your son if it helps. It is designed to be readable by a young person.

Male puberty typically begins between the ages of 9 and 14 — and the wide range is normal. Beginning earlier or later than peers does not indicate anything is wrong.

What happens, roughly in order:

  • Growth of the testicles and scrotum — usually the first sign
  • Pubic hair appears, followed by underarm and facial hair
  • The penis grows in length, then width
  • Height increases — often in rapid spurts
  • Muscle mass develops
  • The voice begins to change — this happens gradually and can be unpredictable
  • Skin produces more oil — spots are common and normal
  • Erections become more frequent, including spontaneous erections unrelated to sexual arousal
  • Ejaculation becomes possible — wet dreams (nocturnal emissions) may begin
  • Sweating increases — deodorant becomes part of daily hygiene

The timeline varies enormously between individuals. A boy who starts puberty at nine and a boy who starts at fourteen are both entirely normal. What matters is not the timing — it is that someone has told them what to expect before it happens.

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? The Puberty Timeline and Normalising Variation

The PSHE Association publishes clear guidance on puberty education for boys, emphasising that one of the most important — and most overlooked — elements of puberty conversations is normalising the variation in timing. Boys who develop earlier or later than peers often experience significant anxiety. Being told explicitly that there is no single right age for puberty to begin is one of the most reassuring things a trusted adult can offer.

?? PSHE Association — PSHE Association | Charity and membership body for PSHE education

?? Erections — The Biology

Dr. Andrew Smiler's research on adolescent male development addresses spontaneous erections directly — one of the most common sources of embarrassment and anxiety in pubescent boys. His work emphasises that spontaneous erections are a normal, involuntary physiological response during puberty, unrelated to sexual arousal, and entirely outside a boy's control. Framing this for boys — this is your body doing something automatic, like hiccups — significantly reduces the shame and alarm that can accompany it.

?? Smiler, A. — Challenging Casanova (Jossey-Bass, 2013)

?? Wet Dreams — Why Preparation Matters

Nocturnal emissions (wet dreams) typically begin between ages 11 and 15. Research consistently shows that boys who experience their first wet dream without any prior preparation describe the experience as alarming and isolating. A brief, matter-of-fact conversation beforehand — what it is, why it happens, what to do — entirely changes the experience. This is one of the clearest examples of how a five minute conversation prevents significant unnecessary distress.

?? Masturbation — The Research on Shame

Debby Herbenick at the Kinsey Institute, Indiana University, has produced extensive research on sexual development and shame. Her work is clear: shame attached to masturbation during adolescence does not prevent the behaviour — it simply accompanies it. Boys who grow up with shame around self-stimulation are significantly more likely to carry that shame into adult relationships, affecting intimacy, communication, and sexual wellbeing. The protective factor is straightforward: being told, clearly and without drama, that self-stimulation is normal, private, and not harmful.

?? Herbenick, D. — Sex Made Easy (Rodale, 2012)

?? The Importance of Correct Anatomical Language

NSPCC research and safeguarding guidance consistently emphasises that children and young people who know and use the correct anatomical names for their body parts — penis, testicles, scrotum, erection, ejaculation — carry less shame, are more able to seek help if something is wrong, and have better outcomes in safeguarding situations. Slang and euphemism inadvertently teach children that those parts of the body are shameful or unspeakable.

?? NSPCC — NSPCC | The UK children's charity

?? What Boys Encounter Without This Conversation

The Internet Watch Foundation and the Sex Education Forum both document the reality that in the absence of age-appropriate information from trusted adults, boys seek information elsewhere — most commonly online, and frequently via pornography. Pornography is not sex education. It does not depict consent, communication, or realistic bodies. Boys who build their understanding of sex and relationships primarily from pornography develop distorted expectations that can affect their relationships throughout their lives.

?? Internet Watch Foundation — Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation IWF
?? Sex Education Forum — sexeducationforum.org.uk

?? The Adolescent Brain

Dr. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's research on the adolescent brain at University College London explains the neurological basis for the emotional intensity of puberty. The prefrontal cortex — responsible for reasoning, impulse control, and emotional regulation — is not fully developed until the mid-twenties. During puberty, the brain is undergoing significant reorganisation. Boys in puberty are not being difficult. Their brains are under construction.

?? Blakemore, S.J. — Inventing Ourselves: The Secret Life of the Teenage Brain (Doubleday, 2018)

?? FIVE TIPS — QUICK RECAP

  • Use the correct anatomical language — penis, testicles, erection, ejaculation. Every time. It reduces shame and increases safety.
  • Lead with normalising — "Something that happens to every boy around your age is..." Universal before personal. Always.
  • Mums — you are not disqualified — you need accurate information and the willingness to use it. That is all.
  • Use the car — no eye contact, no escape route, natural start and stop. The single best location for this conversation.
  • Tell them what you wish you'd known — "Nobody told me this. I want to do it differently for you." Simple. Powerful. True.

Topics: resilience, parenting, confidence, education, family relationships, screen time, identity and belonging, personal growth

"She'll know. She'll just know."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This episode is for every parent raising a girl — and particularly for those who weren't given the full picture themselves.

We follow two families: Diane, a mum who grew up in a household where periods were referred to as being poorly and female bodies were managed in silence; and Rob, a dad raising his daughter alone some weekends who wants to be a person she can talk to and isn't sure he knows enough to be that person.

He does. And so do you.

Along the way we cover everything a parent needs to know about female puberty — the timeline, the physical changes, the correct anatomical language including the vulva and clitoris, masturbation and self-exploration, body image, and the social media pressure that is waiting for every girl on the other side of childhood.

All of it named. None of it left out.

?? EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

00:00 Introduction — 1998 and the clitoris
02:00 Diane and Rob — Part One

13:00 Top Tips — what to say and how to say it

?? PUBERTY IN GIRLS — WHAT TO EXPECT AND WHEN

Share this section with your daughter if it helps. It is designed to be readable by a young person.

Female puberty typically begins between the ages of 8 and 13 — earlier on average than male puberty, and with an equally wide range of normal.

What happens, roughly in order:

  • Breast buds appear — small, sometimes tender, beneath the nipples. This is usually the first sign
  • Pubic and underarm hair begins to grow
  • The vulva and vagina develop — the labia may become more prominent
  • Vaginal discharge begins — this is normal, healthy, and the body's way of keeping itself clean
  • Hips widen
  • Height increases — often in a significant growth spurt
  • Skin produces more oil — spots are common and normal
  • Body odour changes — deodorant becomes part of daily hygiene
  • Periods begin — usually between ages 10 and 16, though earlier or later is also normal

The timeline varies enormously between individuals. A girl who starts puberty at eight and a girl who starts at thirteen are both entirely normal. What matters is not the timing — it is that someone has told them what to expect before it happens.

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? The Clitoris — A Brief History

Until 1998, when Australian urologist Dr. Helen O'Connell published the first accurate mapping of the clitoris using MRI, its full anatomy had never been properly documented in medical literature. The clitoris is significantly larger than most anatomy diagrams suggest — most of its structure is internal. Its sole biological function is pleasure. It was consistently omitted from medical textbooks throughout the twentieth century.

This is not a footnote. It is the context for understanding why girls have historically grown up without accurate knowledge of their own bodies — and why naming it correctly, and explaining what it is for, is an act of genuine importance.

?? O'Connell, H.E. et al. — Anatomical Relationship of the Urethra and Clitoris (Journal of Urology, 1998)

?? The Importance of Correct Anatomical Language

Dr. Jennifer Gunter — obstetrician, gynaecologist, and author — writes extensively on the harm caused by anatomical imprecision in the way we talk about female bodies. The consistent use of vagina as a catch-all term for female genitalia renders female anatomy vague and interchangeable in a way that male anatomy is not. Correct language — vulva, vagina, labia, clitoris, urethra — is not clinical pedantry. It is accuracy, and accuracy is respect.

?? Gunter, J. — The Vagina Bible (Piatkus, 2019)

?? Body Literacy and Female Health

Dr. Christiane Northrup's work on female body literacy makes the case that a woman who understands her own body — its anatomy, its cycles, its responses — is fundamentally better equipped to care for herself, to seek help when something is wrong, and to build intimate relationships from a place of knowledge. Body literacy is a health intervention. It begins with the conversations we have with girls before and during puberty.

?? Northrup, C. — Women's Bodies, Women's Wisdom (Piatkus, 2009)

?? Masturbation and Self-Exploration in Girls

Debby Herbenick's research at the Kinsey Institute, Indiana University, documents a significant gap between the information boys and girls receive about self-exploration. Girls are significantly less likely to receive any information about masturbation from a trusted adult, and significantly more likely to carry shame about it as a result. The cultural silence around female pleasure — deeper and more entrenched than the equivalent silence around male pleasure — has real consequences for girls' relationships with their own bodies and their capacity for healthy adult intimacy.

The protective message is simple and identical to the message for boys: self-stimulation is normal, private, and not harmful.

?? Herbenick, D. — Sex Made Easy (Rodale, 2012)

?? Body Image and Social Media Pressure

Plan International UK's research on girls and body image, and the UK government's commissioned Sexualisation of Young People Review by Dr. Linda Papadopoulos, both document the escalating pressure on girls to conform to narrow and unrealistic beauty standards — amplified significantly by social media. The steepest decline in body confidence in girls occurs in early adolescence, precisely when puberty begins. Girls who receive accurate, shame-free information about their bodies from trusted adults are significantly more buffered against this pressure.

?? Plan International UK — Home | Plan International UK
?? Papadopoulos, L. — Sexualisation of Young People Review (Home Office, 2010)
?? Girlguiding Girls' Attitudes Survey — Girlguiding | Help all girls know they can do anything

?? The Adolescent Brain

As in Episode 2 — Dr. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's research at UCL is relevant here too. The emotional intensity of puberty — in girls as in boys — is neurological. The prefrontal cortex is under construction. Mood swings, emotional amplification, and heightened sensitivity are not personality failures. They are biology.

?? Blakemore, S.J. — Inventing Ourselves: The Secret Life of the Teenage Brain (Doubleday, 2018)

?? FIVE TIPS — QUICK RECAP

  • Use the correct anatomical language — all of it — vulva, vagina, clitoris, labia, uterus. Accurate language is respectful language.
  • Don't leave the clitoris out — it exists. It belongs to her. She deserves to know.
  • Dads — you belong in this conversation — your presence tells your daughter that her body is not something to hide from the men who love her.
  • Talk about body image before social media does — name the pressure early and name it often. The counter-narrative has to start at home.
  • Tell her her body belongs to her — this is the foundation of body autonomy, self-respect, and consent. Everything follows from this.

Episode Title: The Woo Cycle with James and Marlou
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, education, identity and belonging, personal growth, sleep and routines, careers
Show Notes:
"Make it sound easy."

— James, age 8, on how to talk to children about periods

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This episode is something very special.

We are joined by two guests — Malou, founder of Period Reality and a previous guest on The Resilient Kid, and her eight year old daughter James, who is, without question, the star of the show.

Together they have written The Woo Cycle — a beautifully illustrated children's book about periods, designed for children aged four to eight, that does something most books for this age group simply don't. It introduces periods not as something scary or shameful, but as part of a natural, monthly cycle. In language that children came up with themselves.

The name? The Woo Cycle came from James herself — a child's beautiful mishearing of the word womb. And the book's central metaphor — the womb making a bed for a baby, and changing the sheets when no baby comes — came not from Malou, but from James, explaining it to her younger sister Bowie at the age of six.

That is the whole point of this episode. That children, when given the space and the information, find their own language. And that language is often better than ours.

This episode is warm, funny, joyful, and deeply practical. James is an eight year old who already knows more about how to talk to children about periods than most adults. And she is not shy about sharing it.

?? LISTENER GUIDANCE

This episode is suitable for children aged 8 and over, ideally listened to alongside a parent or carer. It contains age-appropriate discussion of periods and the menstrual cycle using gentle, child-friendly language. There is no explicit content.

If you would like to listen first before sharing with your child — please do. But we think you will find it is perfectly pitched for the conversation you may have been putting off.

?? EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

02:00 James introduces herself — actor, singer, future famous person
05:00 What is The Woo Cycle? James explains
08:00 The metaphor that started it all — the womb making a bed

?? MEET THE GUESTS

James

Eight years old. Actor, singer, future famous person — her words, and we believe her entirely. James played Hera in Achilles and Zazu in The Lion King the week this episode was recorded — on her birthday. She is co-author of The Woo Cycle, a gifted explainer of complex things, and the reason the word woo exists in the title. She came up with the book's central metaphor at the age of six whilst explaining periods to her younger sister Bowie. We interviewed her first. Remember that.

Malou

Founder of Period Reality, an organisation dedicated to educating about and advocating for living in sync with the natural rhythms of the menstrual cycle. Malou is a previous guest on The Resilient Kid — link to her first appearance in the resources below. She is also James' mum, and the person who had the wisdom to write down what her daughter said and turn it into a book.

Maya Moore

Illustrator of The Woo Cycle. This is her debut illustrated book, and the illustrations are, in Ashley's words, exquisite. Find her work in the links below. Remember this name too.

?? ABOUT THE BOOK

The Woo Cycle is a children's book for ages 4–8 about periods, the menstrual cycle, and the body's natural rhythms.

It tells the story of Lena, a young girl who walks into the bathroom and finds her mum bleeding. Worried, she asks if her mum is hurt. What follows is a gentle, age-appropriate explanation of what periods are, why they happen, and why they are nothing to be afraid of.

The central metaphor — in James' own words:

"The womb is making a bed for a baby. And if no baby comes to stay, it just changes the sheets."

The book also introduces the concept of the cycle — the idea that the body moves through different phases, and that this rhythm is natural and normal. There is a beautiful page with moon phases to introduce the concept of cycles gently, and a page that normalises rest: "Some days Mummy rests. Some days she runs."

The book is designed to be read by parents, carers, grandparents, and educators with children. It has been read by dads to daughters, by parents to sons, and by grandparents who found it gave them the language they had never previously had.

It rhymes. James' favourite example:

"Lena ran to the loo. Mum was bleeding. What should she do?"

?? KEY THEMES AND RESEARCH CONTEXT

?? Starting Early — Why Ages 4–8 Is the Right Time

One of the most consistent findings in research on puberty education is that preparation before puberty begins is significantly more protective than information delivered after the fact. The PSHE Association and Brook both recommend beginning age-appropriate conversations about bodies and cycles in early childhood — well before periods begin — so that when they do, they arrive in a context of knowledge rather than shock.

The Woo Cycle is built on exactly this principle. The target age of four to eight means that girls — and boys — encounter this information years before they need it personally. And as Malou notes, children at this age take new information as simple fact and move on. It is adults who make it complicated.

?? PSHE Association — PSHE Association | Charity and membership body for PSHE education
?? Brook — Sexual Health & Wellbeing - Brook

?? Children Find Their Own Language — And We Should Listen

One of the most striking things about this episode is how consistently James' own language — woo for womb, the room making a bed, changing the sheets — is clearer and more accessible than the clinical language adults reach for. Malou makes the point explicitly: the metaphor in the book did not come from her. It came from James, translating what she had been told into something her younger sister could understand.

This reflects something we talk about across The Resilient Kid — that children are not passive recipients of information. They process it, translate it, and make it their own. Our job is to give them the information. Their job is to find the words that work for them. As James herself said when asked what parents should do: "Make it sound easy."

?? Dads, Boys, and the Wider Conversation

Malou shared something from the research phase of the book that is worth highlighting. Dads who read The Woo Cycle with their daughters reported feeling unexpectedly included in a conversation they had unconsciously assumed belonged to mum. One dad said he was now excited about the possibility that his daughter might come to him with questions.

The book has also been read widely to boys — with, Malou reports, exactly the same response across the board. Boys do not need to have a menstrual cycle to benefit from understanding one. The research on empathy, healthy relationships, and consent all points to the same conclusion: boys who understand female bodies and experiences — from an early age, in age-appropriate terms — are better equipped to be respectful, empathetic partners, friends, and colleagues.

This connects directly to everything we are covering in Season 11. The conversations are not separate. They build on each other.

?? See also: S11E02 — Growing Up Boy | S11E05 — Teaching Consent From the Start

?? Grandparents and Extended Family

Ashley raises a point in this episode that is worth dwelling on. Grandparents — often from a generation where these conversations simply did not happen — can find The Woo Cycle gives them the language and the context to have conversations with grandchildren that they might otherwise have avoided entirely. The book does the heavy lifting. All they have to do is turn the pages.

?? Period Poverty in the UK

For context in show notes and wider conversations — period poverty remains a significant issue in the UK. One in ten girls in the UK has been unable to afford menstrual products. One in seven has struggled to access them. Normalising conversations about periods is not only emotionally protective — it is part of a wider movement to reduce the stigma that makes period poverty harder to address.
