?? KEY TAKEAWAYS FOR PARENTS AND CARERS

Start earlier than you think you need to. Children aged four to eight accept information about the body as simple fact. The embarrassment is ours, not theirs.

Let children find their own language. Give them the information. Trust them to translate it. Listen to what comes back — it is often better than what you gave them.

Dads — this book is for you too. You do not have to leave this conversation to mum. The Woo Cycle gives every adult in a child's life a way in.

Read it to boys as well. Understanding periods is not just for people who will have them. It is for everyone who will share a world with people who do.

Share it with grandparents. It gives a whole generation the language they never had.

When in doubt — make it sound easy. James said so. She's eight and she's right.

Episode Title: Teaching Consent From the Start
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, boundaries, education, screen time, identity and belonging, personal growth
Show Notes:
"By the time we get to the teenage conversation, consent should already be a language a young person has been speaking for a decade."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

Consent is not a teenage conversation. It begins at three years old — in the moment a toddler doesn't want to be hugged and a parent says: you don't have to.

In this episode we follow two families. Sara and Daniel, thoughtful parents who realise they have been talking about bodies without ever talking about who those bodies belong to. And Nadia, a mum whose daughter Chloe came home from school shaken — not because something had happened, but because it nearly had, and Chloe hadn't had the language to name why it felt wrong.

We map the consent conversation from toddlerhood through to the teenage years — what it looks like at each stage, why it matters at each stage, and what the research tells us about what happens when it doesn't happen at all.

This episode is serious. It is also, ultimately, about empowerment. About giving children the most fundamental thing we can: the knowledge that their body belongs to them.

EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

00:00 Introduction — consent is not a teenage conversation
02:00 Sara and Daniel, and Nadia — Part One
07:00 The Research — consent as a language, not a lesson
13:00 Top Tips — teaching consent at every age
16:00 Sara and Daniel, and Nadia — Part Two
20:00 The Bigger Picture — what the statistics tell us
23:00 The Close
24:30 Outro

CONSENT AT EVERY AGE — QUICK REFERENCE GUIDEAges 2–5 — Body Autonomy

  • You don't have to hug or kiss anyone you don't want to
  • Your body belongs to you
  • It's okay to say no to being touched — even by people you love
  • What to say: "You don't have to give grandma a hug. Would you like to wave instead?"

Ages 5–10 — Naming the Principle

  • Nobody has the right to touch you in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable
  • If that happens — with anyone, even someone you know — you will never be in trouble for telling me
  • Secrets about bodies are not okay — surprises are different from secrets
  • What to say: "Your body belongs to you. If anything ever feels wrong — even with someone we know — you can always tell me."

Ages 10–13 — Pressure and Online Safety

  • Pressure is never a good enough reason to do something your gut says no to
  • If someone makes you feel like you'll look bad for saying no, that is the problem — not you
  • Online pressure is still pressure — screenshots last forever and nobody has the right to ask you for photos of your body
  • What to say: "If anyone — online or in person — ever makes you feel like you have to do something with your body to prove something, that is pressure. And pressure is never okay."

Ages 13+ — Mutual Consent and Relationships

  • Consent means everyone involved genuinely wants to be there and is free to say no without any bad consequences
  • Going quiet, changing the subject, or seeming uncertain is not a yes
  • A yes has to be clear, enthusiastic, and freely given — every time
  • What to say: "Consent goes both ways. You have the right to say no at any point — and so does anyone you're ever with."

RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

Body Autonomy as the Foundation of Consent

The NSPCC's Speak Out Stay Safe programme is built on the evidence that the earliest and most effective consent education begins with body autonomy in early childhood — long before any conversation about sex. Children who have been taught that their body belongs to them, that their no is real, and that they will be believed if they report something uncomfortable, are significantly more likely to disclose abuse and significantly more likely to recognise it in the first place.

?? NSPCC — Healthy relationships | NSPCC
?? Talk PANTS — Talk PANTS: Conversation to help keep children safe | NSPCC

The Continuum of Sexual Violence

Professor Liz Kelly's foundational research on the continuum of sexual violence argues that sexual harm does not emerge from nowhere — it exists on a continuum that begins with the normalisation of small boundary violations. Teaching children from the earliest age that their no is real and must be respected is prevention. Not dramatic. Not formal. Daily, small, consistent.

?? Kelly, L. — Surviving Sexual Violence (Polity Press, 1988)

What Consent Education Prevents

Rape Crisis England and Wales data shows that the majority of sexual assaults on young people are perpetrated by someone known to them. The End Violence Against Women Coalition publishes research consistently showing that comprehensive, early consent education — grounded in bodily autonomy and delivered over time — significantly reduces rates of sexual harassment and assault among young people.

?? Rape Crisis England and Wales — Rape Crisis England & Wales | 0808 500 2222
?? End Violence Against Women Coalition — Home | End Violence Against Women

RSE Statutory Guidance

The UK Government's Relationships and Sex Education (RSE) statutory guidance, introduced in 2020 and mandatory in all schools in England, includes consent as a core component of what schools must teach. This is important — but school lessons alone cannot replace the ongoing, age-appropriate conversations a parent can have across a whole childhood.

?? RSE Guidance — Relationships and sex education (RSE) and health education

Practising No — Dr. Nina Burrowes

Dr. Nina Burrowes' trauma-informed research on consent makes a point that should change how every parent thinks about this. One of the most common reasons young people do not say no — even when they want to — is that they have never practised it in a safe context. The parent who has been saying you don't have to hug grandma since their child was three has been giving them something priceless: practice in using the word, and in having it respected.

?? Burrowes, N. — The Courage to Be Me (Dr Nina Burrowes, 2014)

Prevention — The Lucy Faithfull Foundation

The Lucy Faithfull Foundation works on the prevention of sexual harm and is clear that early, comprehensive education — for all young people, not just potential victims — is the most powerful intervention available. Boys need to hear the consent conversation as explicitly as girls. Every young person needs to understand both their own rights and their responsibilities toward others.

?? Lucy Faithfull Foundation — Lucy Faithfull Foundation - Preventing child sexual abuse

?? FIVE TIPS — QUICK RECAP

  • From the very beginning — respect their no. You don't have to hug grandma. Wave instead. That five-second moment is consent education.
  • Primary age — name the principle explicitly. Your body belongs to you. You will never be in trouble for telling me.
  • Pre-teen — name pressure and online pressure specifically. Pressure is never a good enough reason. Online pressure is still pressure.
  • Teens — make it mutual. Consent goes both ways. A yes must be clear, enthusiastic, and free.
  • After something has happened — start now. It is never too late. The conversation you have today still matters.

Episode Title: Let's Talk About Sex — The Parent Guide
Topics: resilience, parenting, school wellbeing, communication, education, family relationships, screen time, personal growth
Show Notes:
“How do I give them something I never had?”

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This is the episode many parents have been both waiting for and quietly dreading.

We follow Gemma—forty-three, mother of a sixteen-year-old son and a thirteen-year-old daughter—who is honest enough to admit that she received almost no sex education herself and has been carrying that gap ever since.

A leaflet about reproduction. A lesson that covered the mechanics and nothing else. A lifetime of questions she had to answer on her own, some of them incorrectly, for longer than she should have had to.

This episode is about what sex actually is—beyond penetration, beyond reproduction, and beyond the narrow definition most of us were handed.

It is about pleasure and why leaving it out of the conversation causes harm. It is about what healthy sex looks and feels like, not just what unhealthy sex looks like. And it is about how to have that conversation with your teenager, even when—especially when—nobody had it with you.

Contraception, STIs, and pornography are each given their own dedicated conversations in follow-up episodes. This episode does one thing, and it does it fully.

?? EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

00:00 Introduction—what your sex education actually covered
02:00 Gemma’s story—Part One
07:00 The Research—what sex actually is and why the fuller picture matters
13:00 Top Tips—how to talk to your teenager about sex
16:00 Gemma’s story—Part Two
20:00 The Bigger Picture—what young people are getting instead
23:00 The Close—knock on the door
24:30 Outro

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? What Sex Actually Is—Beyond Penetration

Professor Kaye Wellings leads the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), the largest and most comprehensive survey of sexual behaviour in the UK.

Her work defines sexual activity across a wide spectrum that includes kissing, touching, oral sex, mutual masturbation, and penetrative sex of various kinds.

A definition of sex limited to penetration excludes significant portions of human experience and leaves young people without the language to describe their own lives.

?? Natsal— Homepage

?? Pleasure Matters—and Its Absence Causes Harm

Dr Emily Nagoski’s research on human sexuality, widely regarded as some of the most important work in the field, argues that sex education focused exclusively on risk teaches young people that sex is fundamentally dangerous.

What young people also need, alongside information about risk, is permission to understand that sex, in the right context, is something human beings enjoy.

They need to know that their own desire and pleasure are not shameful, and that healthy sex is mutual: both people want to be there, and both people’s enjoyment matters equally.

?? Nagoski, E.—Come As You Are (Scribe, 2015)

?? What Young People Actually Want from Sex Education

The Sex Education Forum’s research, gathered directly from young people, consistently finds that they want honesty.

They want to be treated as real people with real questions, and they want information about what healthy sex looks and feels like—not just what to be afraid of.

They are not, in the main, receiving this. The gap between what young people need and what they are getting remains significant.

?? Sex Education Forum— sexeducationforum.org.uk

?? What Young People Are Getting Instead

The Internet Watch Foundation and Brook both document the reality that, in the absence of honest, human sex education from trusted adults, young people may turn to pornography.

Pornography does not show mutual pleasure. It does not show communication, checking in, or realistic bodies.

It shows a performance that bears little relationship to healthy, mutual, human sexuality. Young people who build their understanding of sex from that performance may develop expectations that significantly affect their experiences and relationships.

?? Internet Watch Foundation— Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation
?? Brook— Sexual Health & Wellbeing | Brook

?? FIVE TIPS—QUICK RECAP

  • Broaden your definition—sex is not just penetration. Talk about the spectrum and give them language for the full picture.
  • Include pleasure in the conversation—their desire matters. Healthy sex is mutual, and both people’s enjoyment counts. Say so.
  • Tell them what healthy looks like—not just what unhealthy looks like. Both people want to be there. Both people feel free to stop. There is communication and checking in.
  • Be honest about your own gaps—“I didn’t get this conversation either. I’m trying to do something different.” That honesty builds trust.
  • Make it a series of small conversations—not one big lecture. A thread that continues. A channel that stays open. Ongoing is always better than once.

Episode Title: Hey, This Is For You: Boys - Age 10-13
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, boundaries, education, careers, creativity
Show Notes:
"What is happening to you is normal. All of it."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This episode is different from everything else in Season 11.

It is not for parents. It is for boys — aged ten to thirteen — spoken directly to them, in language that treats them like the real and capable people they are.

It covers puberty from the inside: what is happening, why it is happening, and — crucially — the things that nobody usually warns boys about. Erections that arrive uninvited. Wet dreams. Masturbation. The emotional turbulence that comes alongside the physical changes. And a few things worth knowing about bodies, boundaries, and the fact that what they see online is not an accurate guide to any of it.

It is warm. It is honest. It is never preachy or clinical. It is the episode many of the boys listening will wish someone had given them earlier.

For parents: listen first, then share. Or share and listen together. Or simply leave it on a phone and say — I thought you might find this useful. Any of those work. All of them are a good idea.

?? LISTENER GUIDANCE

This episode is made for young people aged 10 and over.

It contains age-appropriate discussion of puberty, the body, erections, wet dreams, and masturbation — all handled warmly and without shame. There is no explicit sexual content.

Parents — this episode is safe to share. It is designed to complement the conversations you are having at home, not replace them.

?? EPISODE TIMESTAMPS

00:00 Age guidance and welcome
01:00 First things first — you are not weird
03:00 What's actually happening — and why
07:00 The stuff nobody talks about — masturbation and emotions
10:00 A few things worth knowing
12:00 The close
13:00 Outro

?? PUBERTY IN BOYS — QUICK REFERENCE

This section is written so it can be shared directly with a young person.

What puberty is: Your body upgrading itself from a child's body to an adult's body. It is driven by a hormone called testosterone and takes several years.

What happens:

  • Height increases — often in sudden spurts
  • Muscles develop, shoulders broaden
  • Hair grows under arms, around the penis and testicles, and eventually on the face
  • The penis and testicles grow
  • The voice gets lower — it may crack or wobble during the change
  • Skin produces more oil — spots are common
  • Sweating increases — deodorant is important from now on
  • Erections happen more frequently, including randomly and without warning
  • Ejaculation becomes possible — wet dreams may begin

When does it start? Anywhere between 9 and 14. The range is wide and all of it is normal.

What about feelings? Emotions get bigger during puberty. This is neurological — the brain is rebuilding itself. It is not a character flaw. It gets easier.

?? FOR PARENTS — RESEARCH BEHIND THIS EPISODE

?? Why Boys Need This Information Before It Happens

Research by the PSHE Association on puberty education is clear: boys who receive accurate, age-appropriate information about puberty before the changes begin experience significantly less anxiety than those who encounter the changes without preparation. The wide variation in timing — some boys starting as young as nine, others not until fourteen — is a particular source of anxiety that is significantly reduced by simply being told that the range is normal.

?? PSHE Association — PSHE Association | Charity and membership body for PSHE education

?? Wet Dreams — The Case for Preparation

Research consistently shows that boys who experience their first nocturnal emission without any prior preparation describe the experience as frightening and isolating. A brief, matter-of-fact conversation — or in this case, episode — beforehand entirely changes the experience. This is one of the clearest examples in adolescent development of how a small amount of information prevents a significant amount of unnecessary distress.

?? Masturbation — Why We Name It

Debby Herbenick at the Kinsey Institute, Indiana University, has produced extensive research on sexual development and shame. Her work is consistent: shame attached to masturbation during adolescence does not prevent the behaviour. It accompanies it. Boys who are told — clearly, matter-of-factly, without drama — that self-stimulation is normal, private, and not harmful carry significantly less shame into their adult relationships.

?? Herbenick, D. — Sex Made Easy (Rodale, 2012)

?? The Adolescent Brain and Emotional Regulation

Dr. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's research at University College London on the adolescent brain is the foundation of the emotional section of this episode. The prefrontal cortex — responsible for impulse control and emotional regulation — is the last part of the brain to develop, and is not fully complete until the mid-twenties. The emotional turbulence of puberty is neurological, not behavioural. Boys who understand this about themselves are better equipped to manage it.

?? Blakemore, S.J. — Inventing Ourselves (Doubleday, 2018)

?? Online Pornography — A Brief Note

This episode signposts, but does not cover in detail, the issue of pornography and what it gets wrong. A full episode on this topic is coming in a follow-up to Season 11. For now — the Internet Watch Foundation and Brook both document that the majority of boys this age have encountered pornography online, usually without seeking it out. This episode names it briefly and honestly, and signposts that more is coming.

?? Internet Watch Foundation — Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation IWF
?? Brook — http://brook.org.uk

If your son has just listened to this episode — here are a few things that might help.

Don't make it a big moment. A casual "did you listen to that episode?" on a car journey is better than a sit-down conversation. Keep it low-key.

Be available for questions without pushing for them. "If anything came up that you wanted to ask about — I'm around." Then leave it. They will ask when they are ready.

Follow up on the things this episode signposts. Consent, relationships, and sex are all coming in later episodes of this season. You can share those when the time feels right.

Remember — you don't have to have all the answers. "I'm not sure — let me find out" is a completely valid response to any question. What matters is that you stay in the conversation.

Episode Title: Hey, This Is For You: Girls - Age 10-13
Topics: anxiety, resilience, emotional regulation, parenting, boundaries, education, screen time, identity and belonging
Show Notes:
This episode is spoken directly to girls aged ten to thirteen — in language that treats them like the capable, curious, real people they are.

It covers female puberty from the inside: breast development, body hair, discharge, periods in full detail, the correct names for their anatomy including the vulva and clitoris, masturbation and self-exploration, the emotional changes that come alongside the physical ones, body image and what they see online, and a few things about bodies and boundaries that every girl deserves to know.

It is warm. It is honest. It names things that are often left out — and does so without apology and without drama.

For parents:

Listen first, then share. Or share and listen together. Or leave it quietly on a device. However it gets to her — it is worth getting there.

LISTENER GUIDANCE

This episode is made for young people aged 10 and over.

It contains age-appropriate discussion of puberty, the body, periods, vaginal discharge, the vulva and clitoris, and masturbation — all handled warmly and without shame. There is no explicit sexual content.

Parents — this episode is safe to share. It is designed to sit alongside the conversations you are having at home, not replace them.

PUBERTY IN GIRLS — QUICK REFERENCE

This section is written so it can be shared directly with a young person.

What puberty is:

Your body changing from a child's body to an adult's body, driven by hormones. It takes several years and happens gradually.

What happens:

  • Breast buds appear — small, sometimes tender, under the nipples. Usually the first sign
  • Body hair grows under the arms and around the vulva — pubic hair — and leg hair may become more noticeable
  • Body shape changes — hips widen, waist becomes more defined
  • Height increases — often in sudden spurts
  • Skin produces more oil — spots are common
  • Sweating increases and body odour changes — deodorant from now on

Periods — what to expect:

  • Happen roughly every 21–35 days — irregular at first is normal
  • Last between 3–7 days
  • Amount of blood is around 3–5 tablespoons across the whole period — less than it looks
  • Cramping is common — heat packs and gentle movement help
  • Mood changes before a period are hormonal and real
  • Products available: pads, tampons, period pants, menstrual cups — all are valid options

When does puberty start?

Anywhere between 8 and 13. The wide range is entirely normal.

What about feelings?

Emotions intensify during puberty. This is neurological — the brain is rebuilding itself. It is biology, not weakness.

?? FOR PARENTS — RESEARCH BEHIND THIS EPISODE

?? Correct Anatomical Language

NSPCC research and Dr. Jennifer Gunter's work both emphasise the importance of girls knowing the correct names for their own anatomy — vulva, vagina, labia, clitoris, uterus. Correct language reduces shame, increases safety, and gives girls the vocabulary to seek help if something is wrong.

?? NSPCC — NSPCC | The UK children's charity
?? Gunter, J. — The Vagina Bible (Piatkus, 2019)

?? The Clitoris — Why We Name It

As discussed in Episode 3, the full anatomy of the clitoris was not accurately mapped in medical literature until 1998. Girls who are not told it exists — and that it exists for their pleasure — receive an implicit message that their pleasure does not matter. This episode names it clearly, briefly, and matter-of-factly.

?? Vaginal Discharge — The Case for Preparation

Vaginal discharge typically begins six to twelve months before a girl's first period. Research consistently shows that girls who encounter discharge without any prior information find it alarming. Like wet dreams in boys, this is an area where a small amount of prior information prevents a significant amount of unnecessary distress.

?? Periods — The Research

Dr. Lara Briden's evidence-based work on menstrual health, and Dr. Jen Gunter's period guidance, both emphasise that girls deserve accurate, detailed information about their menstrual cycle before it begins. Preparation significantly reduces anxiety around first periods. Knowledge of the full range of period products available — pads, tampons, period pants, menstrual cups — gives girls agency over their own experience from the start.

?? Briden, L. — Period Repair Manual
?? NHS — Periods — Periods
?? Brook — Periods Archives - Brook

?? Period Poverty

One in ten girls in the UK has been unable to afford menstrual products. Every school in England is required to provide free period products under the Department for Education's Period Products scheme. If a young person is struggling to access products — at school or at home — support is available.

?? _Bloody Good Period — _bloodygoodperiod.com
?? Free Periods — Free Periods
?? DfE Period Products scheme — Welcome to GOV.UK

?? Masturbation and the Gender Gap

Debby Herbenick's research at the Kinsey Institute documents a significant gap between the information boys and girls receive about self-exploration. Girls are much less likely to receive any information about masturbation from a trusted adult, and more likely to carry shame about it as a result.

?? Herbenick, D. — Sex Made Easy (Rodale, 2012)

?? Body Image and What They See Online

Plan International UK's research and the Girlguiding Girls' Attitudes Survey both document the significant and escalating impact of social media on girls' body image during early adolescence. This episode names it directly and honestly.

?? Plan International UK — Home | Plan International UK
?? Girlguiding Girls' Attitudes Survey — Girlguiding | Help all girls know they can do anything

?? The Adolescent Brain

Dr. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's research at UCL is the foundation of the emotional section of this episode. The emotional intensity of puberty is neurological, not behavioural.

?? Blakemore, S.J. — Inventing Ourselves (Doubleday, 2018)

?? FOR PARENTS — AFTER SHE'S LISTENED

If your daughter has just listened to this episode — a few things that might help.

Don't make it a big moment. A casual mention on a car journey — "did you get a chance to listen to that episode?" — is better than a formal sit-down. Keep it light.

Be available without pushing. "If anything came up that you wanted to ask about — I'm here." Then leave it open. She will ask when she is ready.

Follow up on the things this episode signposts. Episode 4 — The Woo Cycle — goes into periods in much more detail and is brilliant. Episodes 9 and 10 cover consent and sex for older teens when the time is right.

Make sure she has period products available. A small pouch in her school bag with a couple of pads and a spare pair of underwear — from around age ten — is a practical and caring thing to do. It tells her you have thought about her and she is prepared.

Notice if she goes quiet rather than asking questions. Some girls will ask directly. Others will go quiet and think. Both are fine. Check in gently a day or two later.

Remember — you don't have to have all the answers. "I'm not sure — let me find out and come back to you" is a completely valid response. What matters is staying in the conversation.

Episode Title: Consent: What It Actually Means 13+
Topics: anxiety, resilience, parenting, school wellbeing, mindfulness, education, screen time, personal growth
Show Notes:
"Consent is not the absence of a no. It is the presence of a yes."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This episode is spoken directly to young people aged thirteen and over.

It covers what consent actually means — not the textbook version but the real, practical version that is useful in actual life. What a genuine yes looks like. What pressure sounds like. How consent applies online. What sextortion is and what to do if it happens. Why consent goes both ways. And what to do if something has already happened that didn't feel right.

It is honest, warm, and direct. It treats young people as the capable people they are. And it ends with a clear message for anyone who is carrying something difficult — it was not your fault, and you do not have to carry it alone.

For parents: this is a good episode to share with your teenager. Listen first so you know what is in it. Then share it — or use it as the starting point for your own conversation.

?? LISTENER GUIDANCE

This episode is for young people aged 13 and over.

It contains discussion of consent, pressure, relationships, online image sharing, non-consensual intimate image sharing, and sextortion. It does not contain explicit sexual content but deals with serious topics in a direct and honest way.

If something in this episode brings something up for a young person — the resources below are there for them.

?? CONSENT — QUICK REFERENCE FOR YOUNG PEOPLE

This section is written so it can be shared directly with a young person.

Consent means:

  • Everyone involved genuinely wants to be there
  • Nobody is being pressured, guilted, or worn down
  • The yes is real, enthusiastic, and freely given
  • Anyone can change their mind at any point — and that has to be respected immediately
  • Yes to one thing is not yes to everything
  • Yes once is not yes always

Pressure sounds like:

  • "If you really liked me you would"
  • "Everyone else does it"
  • "You said you would"
  • "I won't tell anyone"
  • "We've been together long enough"

Pressure is never a good enough reason to do anything. If you feel pressured — that is the problem, not you.

Online consent:

  • Nobody has the right to ask for intimate images of your body — ever
  • Sending an image is not permission for it to be shared
  • Non-consensual intimate image sharing is illegal in the UK
  • Pressure online is still pressure — you are allowed to say no, block, and tell someone

Sextortion — what it is and what to do:

  • Sextortion is when someone uses an intimate image — or the threat of sharing one — to demand money, more images, or other things
  • It is a crime. It is not your fault. It happens to many young people
  • Do not pay. Do not send more images. Do not delete the messages
  • Tell a trusted adult immediately and report to CEOP and the platform

If something has happened:

  • It was not your fault
  • You are allowed to tell someone
  • You will not be in trouble
  • Help is available — see resources below

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? What Consent Education Prevents

Rape Crisis England and Wales and the End Violence Against Women Coalition both publish research showing that comprehensive, ongoing consent education significantly reduces rates of sexual harassment and assault among young people. This is protective for everyone — not just potential victims.

?? Rape Crisis England and Wales — Rape Crisis England & Wales
?? End Violence Against Women Coalition — Home | End Violence Against Women

?? Sextortion — The Scale of the Problem

Sextortion — the use of intimate images or the threat of sharing them to extort money or compliance — is a rapidly growing crime affecting young people in the UK and globally. The Internet Watch Foundation and CEOP both document significant increases in cases involving young people, including cases where the perpetrators are organised criminal networks operating internationally. Young people are targeted deliberately and systematically. Awareness is the most powerful protective factor.

?? _CEOP — _ceop.police.uk
?? Internet Watch Foundation — Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation IWF
?? Revenge Porn Helpline — Revenge Porn Helpline - 0345 6000 459 | Revenge Porn Helpline | 0345 6000 459

?? Online Image Sharing and the Law

Under the Online Safety Act 2023 and existing legislation in England and Wales, non-consensual sharing of intimate images is a criminal offence. Sharing an intimate image of someone without their consent — regardless of how it was obtained — is illegal. Where the person in the image is under eighteen, additional and more serious criminal offences apply.

?? Internet Watch Foundation — Eliminating Child Sexual Abuse Online | Internet Watch Foundation IWF
?? Childline — Childline | Free counselling service for kids and young people | 0800 1111
?? Revenge Porn Helpline — Revenge Porn Helpline - 0345 6000 459 | Revenge Porn Helpline | 0345 6000 459

?? Pressure and Coercion

Dr. Nina Burrowes' work on consent and trauma makes clear that going along with something because the pressure made saying no feel too hard is not consent — even if the word no was never said. Young people need to hear this explicitly, because the cultural narrative around pressure — that persistence is romantic, that wearing someone down is just how it works — is persistent and harmful.

?? Burrowes, N. — The Courage to Be Me

?? RSE Statutory Guidance

The UK Government's Relationships and Sex Education statutory guidance (2020) requires schools to teach consent as part of RSE. This episode is designed to complement and reinforce what young people are taught in school — and to say it in a way that feels more human and more useful than a classroom lesson alone can always achieve.

Written for teenagers in accessible language. Recommended background reading for parents wanting to go deeper on the online safety content in this episode.

Episode Title: Let's Actually Talk About Sex - For 16+
Topics: resilience, parenting, communication, education, screen time, identity and belonging, relationships
Show Notes:
"Your body belongs to you. Your desire is not shameful. Healthy sex is mutual, communicative, and good for everyone involved."

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS ABOUT

This is the final episode of Season 11 — and the most direct.

Addressed to young people aged sixteen and over, this episode covers what sex actually is beyond the narrow definition most people were given, what healthy sex actually looks like, what pornography gets wrong and why it matters, and practical information about contraception and STIs.

It is honest, warm, and completely shame-free. It treats older teenagers as the capable adults they are becoming. And it ends the season the same way it began — by saying the things that needed to be said, clearly, to the people who needed to hear them.

For parents: please listen to this episode before sharing it with your teenager. It is explicit in places and intentionally so. If you decide to share it — good. If you want to listen together — even better.

?? LISTENER GUIDANCE

This episode is for young people aged 16 and over.

It contains direct and honest discussion of sex, pornography, contraception, and STIs. It is the most explicit episode in the season. The content is age-appropriate for sixteen and over and is delivered without shame or sensationalism.

If you are under sixteen — Episodes 7, 8, and 9 are made for you. Come back to this one when you are ready.

?? QUICK REFERENCE — FOR YOUNG PEOPLE

What healthy sex looks like:

  • Both people genuinely want to be there
  • Both people feel free to stop at any point without consequence
  • Both people's pleasure matters equally
  • Communication is part of it — checking in, asking, noticing
  • It does not leave you feeling ashamed or worse about yourself

What pornography gets wrong:

  • Bodies — not representative of real bodies
  • Consent — almost never shown accurately
  • Pleasure — particularly female pleasure, consistently misrepresented
  • What is normal — extreme acts presented as standard

Contraception options:

  • Condoms — the only method that also protects against STIs
  • The pill — taken daily, does not protect against STIs
  • Long-acting reversible contraception — implant, coil, injection — highly effective, free on NHS
  • Emergency contraception — available free from sexual health clinics and some pharmacies, most effective taken as soon as possible

STIs — what to know:

  • Most have no obvious symptoms
  • Condoms significantly reduce risk
  • Testing is free, easy, and confidential — sexual health clinics, GP, or free NHS home testing kits
  • Most STIs are easily treated — what matters is finding out

?? RESEARCH & CONCEPTS MENTIONED

?? What Sex Actually Is — Beyond Penetration

Professor Kaye Wellings leads the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) — the largest and most comprehensive survey of sexual behaviour in the UK. Her work defines sexual activity across a wide spectrum. A definition limited to penetration excludes significant portions of human experience and leaves young people without language for their own lives.

?? Natsal:
https://www.natsal.ac.uk/

?? Healthy Sex and the Role of Pleasure

Dr. Emily Nagoski's research on human sexuality argues that sex education focused exclusively on risk — without any acknowledgement of pleasure — teaches young people that sex is fundamentally dangerous. Healthy sex education includes the understanding that sex, in the right context, is something humans enjoy, and that both people's pleasure matters equally.

?? Nagoski, E. — Come As You Are (Scribe, 2015)

?? Pornography and Young People

The Internet Watch Foundation and Brook both document the reality that the majority of young people in the UK have encountered pornography before receiving any meaningful sex education from a trusted adult. Research by Professor Kaye Wellings and the Sex Education Forum consistently shows that young people who receive accurate, honest sex education from trusted adults are significantly better equipped to contextualise what they see in pornography and to develop healthy sexual expectations.
